findings.title: Snapshot restore: a wildcard body index list is authorized with zero grants, then destroys every index it matches
findings.description: authorize_expression() early-returns Ok(()) for ANY index pattern that cannot reach the reserved `.xerj-memory-` namespace, because restore is classified PatternExpansion::Unguarded: `if expansion == PatternExpansion::Guarded || !may_reach_reserved(expr) { return Ok(()); }`. The SnapshotRestore privilege is only demanded when the body names nothing (authz.rs:1632). Engine::restore_snapshot then expands that pattern against the SNAPSHOT MANIFEST — not the caller's visible set — and for each match runs std::fs::remove_dir_all on the index directory and rewrites it from the snapshot (engine/engine.rs:4503-4546). Result: a Scoped key holding only `read` on `logs-*` can roll back or wipe any other tenant's index it can name with a wildcard. Dynamically verified on a live node with an admin key and a minted `read logs-*` key: POST /_snapshot/repo1/snap1/_restore {"indices":"victim-secret"} -> 403, but {"indices":"v*"} -> 200 and {"indices":"ten*"} -> 200 (no grant on either prefix). The restore rolled `victim-secret` back to snapshot state, silently deleting a document written after the snapshot (count 2 -> 1). Bare "*" is correctly refused only because may_reach_reserved("*") is true; every other wildcard shape passes.
findings.attack_scenario: Any authenticated API key holder — including the most narrowly-scoped tenant key with a single read grant on an unrelated pattern — destroys or rolls back every non-reserved index on the node, cross-tenant, silently. Requires an existing snapshot repo + snapshot, i.e. the normal operator backup state.
findings.exploit_sketch: 1) Operator has PUT /_snapshot/repo1 and a snapshot snap1. 2) Attacker holds a key with role_descriptors granting only read on logs-*. 3) POST /_snapshot/repo1/snap1/_restore with body {"indices":"v*"} (or "ten*", "[a-z]*", "?*") -> HTTP 200 accepted; matching index directories are remove_dir_all'd and rewritten to snapshot state, discarding all writes since the snapshot.

findings.title: slice.max u32 truncation causes a divide-by-zero panic that aborts the whole node — reachable by an untrusted read-only share guest
findings.description: search_impl reads slice.id/slice.max as i64 from the request body and guards `max > 0 && id >= 0 && id < max`, but then casts to u32 before the arithmetic: `(shard % (max as u32))`. max = 4294967296 (2^32) passes the i64 guard and truncates to 0, so `0 <= shards` selects the first branch and `shard % 0` panics. The release profile sets `panic = "abort"` (engine/Cargo.toml:165) and there is no CatchPanicLayer or catch_unwind on this path, so the panic kills the process — every index, the console, all tenants. Dynamically verified twice, including end-to-end with the lowest-privilege principal that exists: created a share via POST /_share, claimed it UNAUTHENTICATED via POST /_share/claim to obtain a guest key, confirmed the guest is correctly confined (403 on /_cat/indices, 403 on another index, 403 on DELETE), then sent one search request and the node died: `thread 'xerj-rt' panicked at crates/xerj-api/src/es_compat.rs:12592:25: attempt to calculate the remainder with a divisor of zero`, process gone.
findings.attack_scenario: An external, untrusted recipient of a read-only share link (who by design should only be able to read one corpus) kills the entire node with a single request. Also reachable by any key with read on any index, or with no credential at all on an --insecure node. Repeatable at will; restart does not help.
findings.exploit_sketch: POST /{any-readable-index}/_search  Content-Type: application/json  {"query":{"match_all":{}},"size":1,"slice":{"id":0,"max":4294967296}}  — connection drops, process aborts.

findings.title: reformat_docvalue byte-slices and truncates a String without a char-boundary check — one stored string value aborts the node
findings.description: reformat_docvalue() is applied to EVERY value resolved from _source for a docvalue_fields entry, with no mapping or type check. For the `strict_date_optional_time`/`date_optional_time` formats it does `frac[..4].to_string()`; for the `*_nanos` / SSSSSSSSS patterns it does `digits.truncate(9)`. Both panic when the byte offset lands inside a multi-byte UTF-8 character. frac is the text from the first '.' to the next 'Z'/'+'/'-', so a value like `x.abé` yields frac = ".abé" (5 bytes) and frac[..4] cuts into the 2-byte é. Dynamically verified: indexing {"d":"x.abé"} and searching with docvalue_fields [{"field":"d","format":"strict_date_optional_time"}] produced `panicked at crates/xerj-api/src/es_compat.rs:38715:33` and, with panic=abort, killed the process. The truncate(9) sibling site (line 38745) is reached the same way with a value of the form `x.abcdefghé` under strict_date_optional_time_nanos.
findings.attack_scenario: Split trigger: any writer (including a low-privilege ingest key, or an autoindexed corpus file) plants an ordinary-looking string containing '.' followed by two characters and a multi-byte character; any reader whose client requests docvalue_fields with a date format — including a read-only share guest, since _search is in GUEST_INDEX_OPS — kills the node. Real corpora hit this accidentally (filenames, URLs, non-ASCII text).
findings.exploit_sketch: 1) PUT {"d":"x.abé"} (raw bytes 78 2e 61 62 c3 a9) into any index.  2) POST /{index}/_search {"query":{"match_all":{}},"docvalue_fields":[{"field":"d","format":"strict_date_optional_time"}]}  -> node aborts.

findings.title: The .seg footer is excluded from the segment CRC and its section_table_offset is never bounds-checked — 8 bytes of data-dir tamper bricks the node permanently
findings.description: from_mmap() computes the integrity CRC over `data[..footer_start]` only — the entire 32-byte footer, which contains section_table_offset, is unauthenticated. It then slices with that value unchecked: `let st_start = section_table_offset as usize; Cursor::new(&data[st_start..])`. The writer always emits 64, so any out-of-file value is pure corruption that still passes the integrity gate. Dynamically verified: after writing 0x0000_0100_0000_0000 into bytes [len-32, len-24) of one .seg (leaving the CRC field and trailing 'BEEZ' magic untouched), the node aborted on boot with `panicked at crates/xerj-storage/src/segment.rs:638:52: range start index 1099511627776 out of range for slice of length 228`, and three consecutive restarts each aborted the same way (from the merge threads) — a permanent crash loop requiring manual filesystem surgery. The section table entries themselves (section()/section_checked(), lines 673-689) are likewise used as raw slice offsets without validation against mmap.len().
findings.attack_scenario: An attacker who can tamper with files in the data directory (malicious snapshot repo contents, compromised backup restore, another local user, a supply-chain-style corpus drop) converts 8 bytes of write access into permanent total denial of service of every index on the node. Because the corrupted value lives in the CRC-excluded footer, the file's integrity check reports it as healthy.
findings.exploit_sketch: For any <data_dir>/<index>/segments/*.seg of size N: seek to N-32, write a little-endian u64 greater than N (e.g. 2^40), leaving the last 4 bytes as the 'BEEZ' magic. On next boot or first query the node aborts; every subsequent boot aborts identically.

findings.title: Ingest pipeline `set`/`add_field` processors panic on a non-object document body, aborting the node
findings.description: AddFieldPlugin::process and SetPlugin::process do `doc[&self.field] = self.value.clone()`. serde_json's IndexMut<&str> implementation panics on any non-object, non-null top-level value (`cannot access key ... in JSON array/string/number/boolean`). Every single-document ingest path hands an arbitrary serde_json::Value to the pipeline with no is-object check: POST /{index}/_doc (es_compat.rs:2760), PUT|POST /{index}/_doc/{id} (:2892), PUT /{index}/_create/{id} (:3068), the `create` action of /_bulk (bulk.rs:845), POST /v1/indices/{name}/ingest (native.rs:2643), and _reindex/_update_by_query. The asymmetry shows this is an oversight rather than a decision: the bulk `index` action explicitly rejects a non-object body two branches above. Dynamically verified: registering {"processors":[{"set":{"field":"env","value":"prod"}}]} then POST /pipe/_doc?pipeline=p with body `[1,2,3]` aborted the process (`panicked at serde_json-1.0.149/src/value/index.rs:102`). Setting the index's default_pipeline makes every subsequent non-object write to that index fatal.
findings.attack_scenario: Any credential with write on a single index — the lowest common ingest grant, e.g. a Beats/Logstash shipper key — kills the whole node, all tenants, with one malformed request. Pipelines with set/add_field are the two most common ES processor types.
findings.exploit_sketch: PUT /_ingest/pipeline/p {"processors":[{"set":{"field":"env","value":"prod"}}]}  then  POST /{index}/_doc?pipeline=p  with body  [1,2,3]  -> node aborts.

findings.title: hdr.number_of_significant_value_digits is unclamped, so u64 overflow turns the bucket-target computation into an infinite loop that pins a worker forever
findings.description: The percentiles HDR histogram computes `let target = 2u64 * 10u64.pow(hdr_digits); let mut p = 1u64; while p < target { p <<= 1; }` with digits taken verbatim from the request (ES's valid range is 0-5; there is no clamp). In release, overflow-checks are off, so digits=20 makes 10u64.pow(20) wrap to 7766279631452241920 and 2x that = 15532559262904483840, which lies in (2^63, 2^64). p reaches 2^63, then `p <<= 1` wraps to 0, and `0 < target` is true forever — a pure spin with no await point and no fuel budget, so the request never returns and the worker is permanently consumed. A twin of the same code exists at es_compat.rs:6542. Dynamically verified on a one-document index: the request never completed in 35s (curl exit 28) and again in 30s, while the node consumed a steady ~92% of one core; other requests continued to be served, so the damage is silent until enough workers are pinned. The loop body runs before any data check, so an empty index is sufficient.
findings.attack_scenario: Any key with read on any index — including a read-only share guest, since this rides in the _search body — pins a tokio worker permanently per request. A handful of requests pins every worker and freezes the node's entire query capacity with no crash, no log line, and no recovery short of restart.
findings.exploit_sketch: POST /{index}/_search {"size":0,"aggs":{"p":{"percentiles":{"field":"v","hdr":{"number_of_significant_value_digits":20}}}}} — repeat a few times against an empty index to consume all workers.

findings.title: The .dv doc-values reader allocates from unvalidated on-disk length fields, and .dv files carry no checksum at all
findings.description: decode_columns() reads `payload_len` as a raw u64 and immediately does `vec![0u8; payload_len]` before read_exact has any chance to bound it — `payload_len > isize::MAX` is a capacity-overflow panic and any large-but-plausible value (1 TiB) is an allocation failure, which aborts the process under panic=abort. name_len (u32, line 1017) is the same shape. NumericColumn::decode/KeywordColumn::decode repeat it with u32 fields: bitmap_len, Vec::with_capacity(doc_count), sorted_len, num_terms (lines 409/413/429/459/466/794/805/818). Additionally line 515-517 `for doc_id in &null_bitmap { data[doc_id as usize] = 0; }` indexes a doc_count-bounded buffer with ids from an attacker-supplied RoaringBitmap and no bounds check — an out-of-bounds write-shaped panic on the query path. Unlike .seg, .dv sidecars are fs::read with no checksum whatsoever, so there is no integrity gate to defeat; the reader is reached lazily per query via Index::read_doc_values_sidecar (xerj-engine/src/index.rs:25758) through dv_columns_for.
findings.attack_scenario: An attacker with data-dir write access (malicious snapshot repo, tampered backup, another local user) flips a handful of bytes in any <data_dir>/<index>/segments/*.dv and gets an immediate process abort on the first sort/aggregation/docvalue read touching that segment — and, since the file persists, a crash loop as in F4.
findings.exploit_sketch: In a .dv file, overwrite the 8-byte little-endian payload_len of any column with 0x0000_0100_0000_0000 (1 TiB). The next query that needs doc values for that field aborts the node.

findings.title: Unbounded recursion on request-controlled dot-paths — stack overflow, which panic=unwind cannot catch
findings.description: Two recursive walks over dot-separated paths have no depth cap and no request-size limit on the paths that feed them. (1) set_source_path() recurses once per segment of the LHS of a scripted update: `let child = obj.entry(path[0].clone()).or_insert_with(|| json!({})); set_source_path(child, &path[1..], value);`. It is fed by consume_source_path() (line 19898), which splits an attacker-written `ctx._source.a.a.a... = 1` left-hand side with no segment limit, reached from apply_one_update_stmt -> update_doc (19751). Unlike _scripts/painless/_execute, which caps source at MAX_SCRIPT_BYTES, the _update body has no size cap beyond the router-wide body limit. (2) expand_dotted_keys/insert_nested (16423/16457) recurse per dot segment of a DOCUMENT KEY whenever the query parameter force_synthetic_source=true is set (16254), so a single _source key of "a.a.a...a" (~100 KB, one JSON level) makes every read with that flag recurse to the same depth. Both sibling helpers (insert_synthetic_path 5749, set_dotted_path 30247) are iterative, confirming these two were missed. A stack overflow raises SIGSEGV/stack-guard abort rather than a Rust panic, so the painless fault-capture wrapper at 19782 cannot catch it.
findings.attack_scenario: A key with write on one index (case 1) or a malicious document author plus any reader who sets force_synthetic_source=true (case 2) crashes the whole node with a single request; a stack overflow is not catchable, so this is the same whole-process kill as F2/F3/F5.
findings.exploit_sketch: POST /{index}/_update/{id} {"script":{"source":"ctx._source.<'a.' repeated ~50000 times>a = 1","lang":"painless"}} — or index {"a.a.a...a":1} and then GET /{index}/_search?force_synthetic_source=true.

findings.title: Term suggester runs full Levenshtein per dictionary term with no length pre-filter and computes it twice
findings.description: The term suggester allocates a full (m+1)x(n+1) DP matrix per (dictionary term, token) pair — `let mut dp = vec![vec![0usize; n + 1]; m + 1];` in suggest_edit_distance (25447) — where n is one whitespace token from suggest.<name>.text (bounded only by the 100 MiB router body limit) and m is a dictionary term. Keyword field values come back verbatim via all_keyword_values_for_field (xerj-engine/src/index.rs:25001), so a corpus can seed very long terms. There is no |m-n| > max_edits bail, no length pre-filter (the distance is computed before being compared to max_edits, so even max_edits:0 pays full cost), and the distance is computed twice per pair — once in a filter() closure and once in the following map() (25759-25772). A 1 MB token against a 100k-term dictionary is ~4e12 character operations; a single large (term, token) pair first attempts a multi-gigabyte vec! allocation, which aborts under panic=abort. Because suggest rides in the _search body, this is reachable by any read-only key and by read-only share guests (GUEST_INDEX_OPS contains _search and only the pit/scroll params are denied).
findings.attack_scenario: A read-only share guest or low-privilege reader sends one search whose suggest.text contains a very long single token, stalling the node for minutes or aborting it on the allocation — while authz correctly reports the guest as able to do nothing else.
findings.exploit_sketch: POST /{index}/_search {"size":0,"suggest":{"s":{"text":"<one ~1 MB token with no whitespace>","term":{"field":"body"}}}} against an index with a populated keyword/text field.

findings.title: GET /_snapshot/{repo} returns stored repository settings verbatim, including absolute filesystem paths, to any authenticated key with zero grants
findings.description: The snapshot-repo GET handler echoes each stored repo body back unchanged. Reads under /_snapshot are classified Target::Cluster + cluster_is_read, which is permitted to every authenticated principal with no privilege check, and prune_sites has no _snapshot entry — so a key with a single read grant on an unrelated pattern reads the operator's repo configuration, including settings.location, which is an absolute path inside the node's data_dir. Dynamically verified with a key whose only grant was read on logs-*: GET /_snapshot/repo1 returned {"repo1":{"type":"fs","settings":{"location":"/root/ab-run-p2/scratch-auth-9950/snaps"}}}. This discloses the data directory's absolute location and the existence/naming of backup infrastructure to every tenant. (PUT /_snapshot/{repo} is, by contrast, correctly superuser/Unscoped-only.)
findings.attack_scenario: Any authenticated API key, however narrowly scoped — including keys minted for third-party shippers or dashboards — learns the node's absolute data_dir layout and snapshot topology, useful reconnaissance for the data-dir and path-traversal classes above.
findings.exploit_sketch: With a key granted only read on logs-*: GET /_snapshot/repo1  (or /_snapshot/_all)  -> 200 with the absolute location path in the body.

method_note: I mapped the attack surface from the two routers (which routes exist, which middleware runs and in what order), then audited each focus area in parallel with subagents covering es_compat.rs, the xerj-wasm ingest pipeline, the xerj-storage/xerj-engine persistence readers, and the console/SPA. I then personally re-derived and dynamically verified every high-severity claim against a prebuilt release binary, booting fresh nodes per test. Dynamically confirmed: the authz wildcard-restore bypass (literal 403 vs wildcard 200, data actually rolled back), the slice.max divide-by-zero (including end-to-end from an unauthenticated /_share/claim guest key that was 403 on everything else), the docvalue_fields char-boundary panic, the .seg footer tamper causing a three-restart crash loop, the pipeline non-object panic, the HDR infinite loop at ~92% of a core, and the snapshot repo path leak. I also tried to reproduce the reported _clone escalation; it did not reproduce (index_guard held), so I excluded it. Static-only findings are marked medium confidence.
